Summary
Although surrogate measures to quantify pain intensity have been commercialised, there is a need to
develop a new index with improved accuracy. The aim of this study was to develop a new analgesic index
using nasal photoplethysmography data. The specially designed sensor was placed between the columella
and the nasal septum to acquire nasal photoplethysmography in surgical patients. Nasal photoplethysmog-
raphy and Surgical Pleth Index /C226(GE Healthcare) data were obtained for 14 min both in the absence (pre-
operatively) or presence (postoperatively) of pain in a group of surgical patients, each patient acting as
their own control. Various dynamic photoplethysmography variables were extracted to quantify pain inten-
sity; the most accurate index was selected using logistic regression as a classi ﬁer. The area under the curve
of the receiver-operating characteristic curve was measured to evaluate the accuracy of ﬁnal model predic-
tions. In total, 12,012 heart beats from 89 patients were used to develop a new Nasal Photoplethysmogra-
phy Index for analgesic depth quanti ﬁcation. The two-variable model (a combination of diastolic peak
point variation and heart beat interval variation) was most accurate in discriminating between the presence
and absence of pain (numerical rating scale (NRS) ≥ 3). The accuracy and area under the curve of the recei-
ver-operating characteristic curve for the Nasal Photoplethysmography Index were 75.3% and 0.8018,
respectively, and 64.8% and 0.7034, respectively, for the Surgical Pleth Index. The Nasal Photoplethysmog-
raphy Index clearly distinguished pain (NRS ≥ 3) in awake surgical patients with postoperative pain. The
Nasal Photoplethysmography Index performed better than the Surgical Pleth Index. Further validation stud-
ies are needed to evaluate its feasibility to quantify pain intensity during general anaesthesia.

Introduction
Accurate assessment and treatment of pain is critical in
peri-operative care because pain signi ﬁcantly affects
postoperative patient outcome [1, 2]. Commercial anal-
gesic indices have been developed for use in clinical set-
tings to quantify acute pain, irrespective of patient

cooperation [3 –5]. Among them, the Surgical Pleth Index
(GE Healthcare, Milwaukee, WI, USA) is widely used; this
index quanti ﬁes intra-operative pain using photoplethys-
mography acquired from an index ﬁnger [6]. Surgical
Pleth Index is superior to hemodynamic variables, such as
heart rate and blood pressure, in quantifying pain inten-
sity during general anaesthesia [7 –9], but its accuracy can
be improved. Furthermore, Surgical Pleth Index fails to
quantify acute postoperative pain with more than moder-
ate-to-low sensitivity and speci ﬁcity [10]. Its baseline varia-
bility in the SPI is so large that it is doubtful whether an
absolute value on this scale can distinguish pain as a sur-
rogate measure of analgesic depth [11]. Thus, there is a
need for the development of a new surrogate measure of
analgesic depth.
Photoplethysmography, which is plethysmography
obtained using optical technique, measures the change
in the volume of arterial blood with each pulse beat [12].
Photoplethysmography sensors are usually placed on an
upper extremity; pulsatile ﬂow at this site is vulnerable in
patients who exhibit compromised peripheral perfusion
[13, 14]. In these patients, the use of nasal photoplethys-
mography may be a viable alternative, as much of the
blood supply to the nasal area originates from a polygo-
nal system connecting the external and internal carotid
arteries [15]. Additionally, nasal photoplethysmography
may be less affected by pain-induced motion artefacts.
The aim of this study was to develop a new analgesic
index using nasal photoplethysmography data, with and
without pain, from the same individual.
Methods
Written informed consent was obtained from each
patient. Patients who were 20 –80 years old (inclusive),
and who were scheduled for elective surgery, were
enrolled if their ASA physical status was 1, 2 or 3. Exclu-
sion criteria were as follows: women who were pregnant
or lactating; clinically signi ﬁcant impairment of cardiovas-
cular, hepatic or renal function; history of cardiac arrhyth-
mia; use of medication that might affect autonomic
function; use of pre-operative analgesic or neuroleptic
medication; the presence of pre-surgical acute or chronic
pain [numerical rating scale (NRS) ≥ 1, measured before
surgery] and history of substance abuse or psychiatric
disease.
All patients fasted beginning at midnight on the day
of surgery, without premedication. Once in the operating
theatre, they were monitored using pulse oximetry, elec-
trocardiography, end-tidal carbon dioxide partial pres-
sure and non-invasive blood pressure. A specially-
designed sensor was placed between the columella and
the nasal septum to acquire nasal photoplethysmography
(Fig. 1). This sensor, and accompanying software that can
download nasal photoplethysmography wave data, were
provided by KTMED Inc. (Seoul, Korea), which manufac-
tures pulse oximeters. A reusable Surgical Pleth Index
sensor (Carescape /C226B850; GE Healthcare, Milwaukee, WI,
USA) was placed on the index ﬁnger of the arm, opposite
to the arm used for blood pressure measurement. Surgi-
cal Pleth Index values were recorded at 10-s intervals on
a laptop computer for of ﬂine analysis. Nasal photo-
plethysmography and Surgical Pleth Index data were
obtained for 14 min after con ﬁrmation that the patient
had no pain. After data collection, general anaesthesia
was induced according to the usual method. Target
effect-site concentrations of propofol were adjusted
within a range of 2.5 /C0 3 lg.ml/C0 1 to maintain bispectral
index (BIS TM, Covidien, Boulder, CO, USA) values of less
than 60 during induction and maintenance of anaesthesia
[16]. Target effect-site concentrations of remifentanil were
titrated to maintain stable haemodynamics (systolic blood
pressure > 80 mmHg; heart rate > 45 beats.min /C0 1) [17].
Tracheal intubation was facilitated by administration of
rocuronium 0.6 mg.kg /C0 1. Patients ’ lungs were then venti-
lated with oxygen in air (1:2), and ventilation rate was
adjusted to maintain an end-tidal carbon dioxide partial
pressure of 4.7 –6.0 kPa. All patients were administered a
bolus dose of oxycodone of 0.1 mg.kg /C0 1, 30 min before
the end of surgery. Intravenous (i.v.) patient-controlled

photoplethysmography sensor placed on the nose. The

analgesia (PCA) with oxycodone was started after admin-
istration of the loading dose. A semi-electronic pump
(Automed 3200; Ace Medical, Seoul, South Korea) was
used with a demand bolus of 1 ml, a background infu-
sion of 1 ml.h /C0 1 and a lock-out time of 15 min. The con-
centration of oxycodone in each i.v. PCA bag was
1 mg.ml /C0 1. Neuromuscular blockade was reversed with
neostigmine and glycopyrrolate at the end of surgery.
Patients were the transported to the recovery area. Addi-
tional nasal photoplethysmography and Surgical Pleth
Index data were obtained for the initial 14 min in the
recovery area. After obtaining these data, patients were
assessed for pain using a numerical rating scale (NRS)
(0 = no pain; 10 = the most severe pain).
Within a 14-min photoplethysmography waveform,
1 min of data containing little or no noise were selected
by an experienced researcher. Considering the possibility
of commercialisation of an analgesic index, and the need
for suf ﬁcient information acquisition to distinguish the
presence of pain, we analysed the 1-min data. Selected
photoplethysmography data were sampled at 300 Hz
and ﬁltered using a third-order bandpass ﬁlter at
0.5/C0 25 Hz. Systolic peak point (SPP) and diastolic peak
point (DPP) were detected by the Matlab ‘ﬁndpeak’ func-
tion with pre-de ﬁned thresholds, such as minimum peak
distance and height. Detected peak position was veri ﬁed
by another experienced researcher and corrected for fal-
sely detected or missed peaks. Matlab 2016a (Math-
works, Inc., MA, USA) was used for all signal analysis
procedures regarding peak detection and development
of an analgesic index [18].
Candidate variables were selected according to the
physiological theory that pain activates the sympathetic
nervous system [19]. Speci ﬁcally, photoplethysmography
amplitudes have arbitrary units because they are in ﬂu-
enced by various factors including: skin colour; human
body composition of measurement site; anatomical struc-
ture; and ambient light [20]. For this reason, photo-
plethysmography amplitudes could not be quanti ﬁed.
Variables related to photoplethysmography amplitude
were normalised via division by the systolic peak ampli-
tude (SPA) of each beat. Variables analysed were nor-
malised pulse area (PA norm = PA SPA /C0 1); systolic peak
variation (Sys var = Sysdiff SPA/C0 1); diastolic peak variation
(Diavar = Diadiff SPA/C0 1); systolic interval variation
(SIvar = SIdiff per unit time); diastolic interval variation
(DIvar = DIdiff per unit time); and heart beat interval varia-
tion (HBI var = HBIdiff per unit time). The unit time of the
variables related to the time interval was set to 1 s.
Graphical representation of these variables is shown in
Fig. 2; variable properties are described here. Systolic
peak amplitude is the difference in amplitude between
current systolic peak point and previous diastolic peak
point; pulse area (PA) is the area under the curve of a
pulse waveform. Sys diff is a difference in amplitude
between current systolic peak point and the next systolic
peak point. Sys var is calculated by dividing Sys diff by sys-
tolic peak amplitude. Dia diff is a difference in amplitude
between two diastolic peak points within a waveform.
Diavar is calculated by dividing Dia diff by systolic peak
amplitude. SI diff is a difference in systolic interval between
the previous diastolic peak point and current systolic
peak point. DI dff is a difference in diastolic interval
between the current systolic peak point and the next
diastolic peak point. HBI diff is a difference in heart beat
interval between the current beat and the next beat.
